title: Quasi-finiteness at a prime descends to an intermediate ring
statement: Let $A\to B$ and $B\to C$ be homomorphisms of commutative rings such that the composite $A\to C$ is of finite type [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra] (then $B\to C$ is of finite type). Let $\mathfrak r\subset C$ be a prime ideal. If $A\to C$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak r$ [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime], then $B\to C$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak r$.

proof.text: *$B\to C$ is of finite type.* Write $\psi:A\to B$, $\chi:B\to C$ and $\varphi=\chi\circ\psi:A\to C$. Since $A\to C$ is of finite type [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra], there are $c_1,\dots,c_n\in C$ such that every element of $C$ is a polynomial in $c_1,\dots,c_n$ with coefficients in $\varphi(A)$. As $\varphi(A)=\chi(\psi(A))\subseteq\chi(B)$, every element of $C$ is a polynomial in $c_1,\dots,c_n$ with coefficients in $\chi(B)$, i.e. the $B$-algebra map $B[x_1,\dots,x_n]\to C$, $x_i\mapsto c_i$, is surjective: $B\to C$ is of finite type. So the statement makes sense.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 0C6H (lemma-quasi-finite-permanence, line 30393), proof, first sentence (citing Lemma Tag 00F4, lemma-compose-finite-type, line 540)

proof.text: *The comparison map of fibre rings.* Put $\mathfrak q=\chi^{-1}(\mathfrak r)\subset B$ and $\mathfrak p=\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak r)=\psi^{-1}(\mathfrak q)\subset A$, prime ideals. For $s\in A\setminus\mathfrak p$ we have $\psi(s)\notin\mathfrak q$, so $A_{\mathfrak p}\to B_{\mathfrak q}$, $a/s\mapsto\psi(a)/\psi(s)$, is a well-defined ring homomorphism [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime]; it maps $\mathfrak pA_{\mathfrak p}$ into $\mathfrak qB_{\mathfrak q}$ (as $\psi(\mathfrak p)\subseteq\mathfrak q$), hence induces a ring homomorphism $\kappa(\mathfrak p)\to\kappa(\mathfrak q)$, $\lambda\mapsto\bar\lambda$, with $\overline{a\cdot\lambda}=\psi(a)\cdot\bar\lambda$ for $a\in A$. Let $F_A=C\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ and $F_B=C\otimes_B\kappa(\mathfrak q)$ be the fibre rings of $A\to C$ over $\mathfrak p$ and of $B\to C$ over $\mathfrak q$ [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime], with $j_A:C\to F_A$, $c\mapsto c\otimes1$, and $j_B:C\to F_B$, $c\mapsto c\otimes1$. The map $C\times\kappa(\mathfrak p)\to F_B$, $(c,\lambda)\mapsto c\otimes\bar\lambda$, is biadditive and $A$-balanced: for $a\in A$, $(\varphi(a)c)\otimes\bar\lambda=(\chi(\psi(a))c)\otimes\bar\lambda=c\otimes\psi(a)\bar\lambda=c\otimes\overline{a\lambda}$. Hence it induces an additive map $\theta:F_A\to F_B$ with $\theta(c\otimes\lambda)=c\otimes\bar\lambda$; it is multiplicative on pure tensors and sends $1\otimes1$ to $1\otimes1$, so it is a ring homomorphism, and $\theta\circ j_A=j_B$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 0C6H (lemma-quasi-finite-permanence, line 30393), proof: 'the primes lying over q form a subset of the primes lying over p', realized by the map of fibre rings; fibre rings as in Remark Tag 00E6 (remark-fundamental-diagram, line 3422)

proof.text: *The point $\mathfrak r$ in both fibres.* By [lem-weil-pbc-fibre-ring-primes-bijection] applied to $\varphi:A\to C$ and $\mathfrak p$, there is a unique prime $\overline{\mathfrak r}_A$ of $F_A$ with $j_A^{-1}(\overline{\mathfrak r}_A)=\mathfrak r$ (as $\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak r)=\mathfrak p$); by the same lemma applied to $\chi:B\to C$ and $\mathfrak q$, there is a unique prime $\overline{\mathfrak r}_B$ of $F_B$ with $j_B^{-1}(\overline{\mathfrak r}_B)=\mathfrak r$ (as $\chi^{-1}(\mathfrak r)=\mathfrak q$). Claim: for a prime $\mathfrak Q$ of $F_B$, $\theta^{-1}(\mathfrak Q)=\overline{\mathfrak r}_A$ if and only if $\mathfrak Q=\overline{\mathfrak r}_B$. Indeed $\theta^{-1}(\mathfrak Q)$ is a prime of $F_A$ and, by step 2, $j_A^{-1}(\theta^{-1}(\mathfrak Q))=(\theta\circ j_A)^{-1}(\mathfrak Q)=j_B^{-1}(\mathfrak Q)$. If $\mathfrak Q=\overline{\mathfrak r}_B$, then $j_A^{-1}(\theta^{-1}(\mathfrak Q))=\mathfrak r$, so $\theta^{-1}(\mathfrak Q)=\overline{\mathfrak r}_A$ by the uniqueness for $\varphi$. If $\theta^{-1}(\mathfrak Q)=\overline{\mathfrak r}_A$, then $j_B^{-1}(\mathfrak Q)=j_A^{-1}(\overline{\mathfrak r}_A)=\mathfrak r$, so $\mathfrak Q=\overline{\mathfrak r}_B$ by the uniqueness for $\chi$. Thus the map $\theta^*:\operatorname{Spec}F_B\to\operatorname{Spec}F_A$, $\mathfrak Q\mapsto\theta^{-1}(\mathfrak Q)$, satisfies $(\theta^*)^{-1}(\{\overline{\mathfrak r}_A\})=\{\overline{\mathfrak r}_B\}$.

source.place: Algebra, Lemma Tag 0C6H (lemma-quasi-finite-permanence, line 30393), proof: the primes of C over q are among those over p; the identification of the primes of a fibre ring with the primes over p is Remark Tag 00E6 (remark-fundamental-diagram, line 3422)

proof.text: *Conclusion.* The map $\theta^*$ is continuous for the Zariski topologies [def-weil-affine-spectrum]: for an ideal $I\subseteq F_A$ and a prime $\mathfrak Q$ of $F_B$, $\theta^*(\mathfrak Q)\in V(I)$ iff $I\subseteq\theta^{-1}(\mathfrak Q)$ iff $\theta(I)\subseteq\mathfrak Q$ iff $\mathfrak Q\in V(\theta(I)F_B)$, so the preimage of a closed set is closed. Since $A\to C$ is of finite type and quasi-finite at $\mathfrak r$ [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime], $\{\overline{\mathfrak r}_A\}$ is open in $\operatorname{Spec}F_A$; hence its preimage $\{\overline{\mathfrak r}_B\}$ (step 3) is open in $\operatorname{Spec}F_B=\operatorname{Spec}(C\otimes_B\kappa(\mathfrak q))$. As $B\to C$ is of finite type (step 1) and $\overline{\mathfrak r}_B$ is the prime of $F_B$ corresponding to $\mathfrak r$, this says by [def-weil-pbc-ring-map-quasi-finite-at-prime] that $B\to C$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak r$.
